The core never talks to a database. It is handed four stores, and any implementation that passes the conformance suite in `@noctcore/auth/testing` is a valid one. `@noctcore/auth-redis` and `@noctcore/auth-prisma` are adapters like any other: both run the same suite against a real Redis and PostgreSQL in CI.

## What each store must guarantee

The interfaces are in `packages/auth/src/ports/stores.ts`, with the guarantee each method gives in its comment. The ones the flows depend on, and that the suite tests under concurrency:

**`UserStore`** (users and password hashes)

- `create` returns `null` when the email is taken, even under 20 concurrent creates of one address. It never throws on a unique violation.
- `setPasswordHash` is guarded: it writes nothing and returns `false` for a missing or soft-deleted user. With `expected`, it is a compare-and-set in one statement, so a rehash on login can never overwrite a password changed meanwhile.
- `markEmailVerified` writes only while the stored email still equals the one given, so a stale code cannot verify a changed address.
- `changeEmail` (optional; the email change flows need it) moves the user from `from` to `to`, marks the address verified and, with `clearPassword`, removes the hash, in one statement guarded on the stored email still equalling `from`. It answers `stale` when that guard fails or the user is missing or soft-deleted, and `taken` when another user (soft-deleted ones included) holds `to`, never throwing on the unique violation: of 10 users racing for one address, exactly one gets `changed`.
- The `find*` methods return live users only: a soft-deleted user is not found.

**`TokenStore`** (one-time codes and links, as hashes)

- `put` keeps one token per user and purpose, replacing the old one; concurrent puts never throw.
- `consume` removes and returns the token atomically: of 50 concurrent callers, exactly one gets it.
- `incrementAttempts` never passes the cap: of N concurrent callers, at most `max` get a number.

**`SessionStore`** (sessions and revocation epochs)

- `touch` replaces a session only if it still exists, keeping its TTL, and never brings back a deleted one, even when racing the delete on another connection.
- `delete` returns the ids it removed (the ones that still existed), so that of two deletes racing on one session exactly one reports it. Evictions, sign-outs and revocations report to `onSessionsRevoked` from this list. A store that returns nothing still works, but a session two of them race on may then be reported twice. Run the conformance suite with `deleteReportsRemoved: false` for such a store: the delete cases are then listed as skipped instead of failing.
- `bumpEpoch` is an atomic increment, and the epoch must outlive every session it guards. A store that can only guard sessions up to some age says so in `maxSessionTtlMs`, and `createAuth` refuses longer sessions. A store that forgets an epoch some time after its last write (and then reads it as 0) says how long in `epochTtlMs`: device cookies and trusted devices are fenced by the epoch alone, so `createAuth` refuses a `throttle.lockout.deviceMaxAge` or a two-factor `trustedDevices.ttl` longer than it. Leave it out when the epoch never lapses.
- Every record expires with its session: the session at its TTL, its index entry with it.

**`CounterStore`** (rate limits and lockout)

- The first `increment` arms the window; later hits never extend it. Concurrent increments each see a distinct count.
- Every key has a TTL, always, so no counter outlives its window.
- `decrement` lowers the count by one, never below 0, keeps the TTL and never creates a missing key.

## A worked example

A `CounterStore` on `node:sqlite`, for a single-process app. Each method is one SQL statement and SQLite runs one statement at a time, which is what makes the increment atomic. On a database shared by several processes the same logic needs a conditional upsert your database runs atomically, as the Redis store does with a script.

## Running the conformance suite

Each suite is a function that takes your store and returns a list of named cases that assert with `node:assert`, so they run under any test runner. `runConformance(title, cases, { describe, it })` registers them with yours. This test runs the counter suite with `node --test`:

<Code code={testTs} lang="ts" title="src/sqlite-counter-store.test.ts" />

Under Vitest or Jest, pass the runner's own functions: `runConformance('my store', cases, { describe, it })`. That is how both shipped adapters do it, in `packages/auth-redis/tests/redis.int.test.ts` and `packages/auth-prisma/tests/prisma.int.test.ts`.

| Suite | Options |
| --- | --- |
| `userStoreConformance(store, options)` | `softDelete(id)`: soft-deletes a user, if your store supports soft deletion. Without it that case is left out. |
| `tokenStoreConformance(store)` | none |
| `sessionStoreConformance(store, options)` | `secondary`: a second instance of your store on its own connection, so the touch-versus-delete race really crosses connections. `epochTtlMs(userId)`: the remaining TTL of a user's epoch, for stores that expire epochs; enables the check that the epoch outlives the longest session. `deleteReportsRemoved: false`: for a store whose `delete` cannot return the ids it removed; the three delete cases are listed as skipped. `advanceTime`, as below. |
| `counterStoreConformance(store, context)` | `advanceTime`, as below. |
| `membershipStoreConformance(store)` | none. For the membership plugin: a role change and a removal apply only to the role the caller decided on, and never leave a scope without an admin, checked with concurrent demotions and removals ([Membership guards](/auth/build/membership/#the-store)). |
| `invitationStoreConformance(store)` | none. For the invitations plugin: `consume` gives an invitation to exactly one of many concurrent callers, and `create` keeps one live invitation per scope and address, also under concurrent creates ([Invitations](/auth/build/invitations/#the-store)). |

The expiry cases move time forward. By default they sleep, which suits a real backend with its own clock. A store built on an injectable `Clock` can pass `advanceTime: (ms) => clock.advance(ms)` with a `manualClock()`, and those cases then run instantly. Start the manual clock at `Date.now()`, because the sample records carry real timestamps.

On a shared backend, every case writes under ids from `uniqueId`, so parallel runs never collide. Give the store a prefix of its own (the Redis tests use `uniqueId('test')`) and remove its keys after the run.

## Switching from your own sessions

An app that already has signed-in users keeps its sessions in its own format, so pointing `stores.sessions` at the package's store signs everyone out. `adoptLegacySessions(store, options)` wraps the package's store instead: a session it does not hold is looked up once in your old store, converted, written to the package's store in its format, and removed from the old one. Every later request is served from the package's store alone.

It works when your old cookie carries a token the package accepts (64 lowercase hex characters, the shape of `generateToken`) under the cookie name the package reads (`session.cookie.name`), and your old store can find a session by the SHA-256 hex of that token, the package's store key. An old store keyed by the raw token can be rekeyed once with a script before the switch. Otherwise, the package cannot recognise the old cookies, and the switch signs those users out.

<Code code={legacyTs} lang="ts" title="src/old-sessions.ts" />

`take(id)` returns the old session as a `LegacySession` (`userId`, `createdAt`, `authenticatedAt`, `lastActiveAt`, `expiresAt`, `idleTimeoutMs`, `rememberMe`, and optionally `persistentCookie`, `ip`, `userAgent` and `attributes`), or `null`. It must remove the record as it reads it, in one atomic step, like `TokenStore.consume`. Report `createdAt` as `authenticatedAt` unless your old store recorded a later sign-in or re-authentication: `authenticatedAt` grants fresh-auth standing, so a later value lets the session change the password or revoke other devices without asking for the password again. What the wrapper does with it:

- **Adopted once.** The old record is gone before the new session is written, so signing out of an adopted session cannot be undone by adopting it again, and of two requests racing on one cookie only one adopts it. The other looks for the session the first is writing, once more after 50 ms, and is refused if that write is still not visible, with the reason `session_adopting` (`adopting` from the session manager) instead of `session_unknown`. That request is answered as signed out, but its cookie is kept: `clearsSessionCookie(result)` is false for it, and both `@noctcore/auth-nestjs` (its CSRF middleware) and `@noctcore/auth-trpc` (its context) clear the session cookie only when that check says so. The browser keeps sending the cookie, and the next request finds the adopted session. An adapter of your own should clear the cookie through the same check. A request on one process cannot see that another process took the record, so every token neither store knows (one revoked or expired since the switch, or made up) is refused this way while the wrapper is installed: refused, never accepted, but its cookie stays until the user signs in again or the wrapper is removed. A malformed token, and an old record the wrapper drops (below), are refused for good and their cookie is cleared. Every cookie neither store knows pays the 50 ms wait on each request while the wrapper is in place.
- **Revocations reach it.** The adopted session carries revocation epoch 0, the epoch of a user whose sessions were never revoked. After a password change or a sign-out everywhere, any old session the user had not used since the switch is refused when it is presented. For the same reason, a user whose epoch was already bumped in the store you switch to loses their old sessions.
- **Never longer.** The session expires at its old expiry, but never later than `maxTtl` after its `createdAt` (or the store's `maxSessionTtlMs`, when shorter). Set `maxTtl` to your `session.rememberMeTtl`. A future `authenticatedAt` or `lastActiveAt` is brought back to now.
- **Dropped, not adopted.** An expired record, one created in the future, or one with a missing user id, a time that is not a number, a zero idle timeout or a non-boolean `rememberMe` is removed and refused. A malformed one is reported to `logger` with the user id only. Attributes go through `session.attributes` like any session's.

Old sessions are not listed in `auth.sessions.list` until they are first used, and the per-user cap counts them from then on.

**Pass the result directly to `createAuth`.** The `adopting` signal lives on the store `adoptLegacySessions` returns, and the session manager reads it from there. A store of your own that wraps that result (to log or count calls) hides it, so a request that loses the race is refused as `session_unknown` and its cookie is cleared: the user is signed out again. To log or count, wrap the package's store first and pass the wrapped store to `adoptLegacySessions`.

**Remove the wrapper once `maxTtl` has passed since the switch.** By then every old session has been adopted or has expired, so the wrapper has nothing left to adopt, but while it is installed every cookie the package's store does not know still costs a read of your old store, a second read of the package's store and the 50 ms wait, and keeps its cookie. Pass the package's store to `createAuth` directly again, then drop the old table.

## In-memory stores

`memoryStores()` from `@noctcore/auth/testing` returns all four stores in memory. They pass the same suite and are meant for unit tests and prototypes: nothing survives a restart and nothing is shared between processes. The fakes beside them (`manualClock`, `plainHasher`, `recordingMailer`, `recordingAudit`) let a unit test drive `createAuth` without Redis, a database or Argon2.
